point_one.text: On the train, I open the For you page before my stop. Topics I follow are near the top, so I can scan headlines instead of searching. The page uses my chosen interests and sources, as well as past activity from other services. I can follow or unfollow a topic, ask for more or less of a story, or hide a source. That gives me a useful feeling: my short morning belongs to me. I still worry that an important story may never reach my screen. With little time, this feels practical. I am not alone: many people in an international survey also found automatic choices based on past preferences comfortable.

point_two.text: Sometimes when I open my feed, I see similar kinds of claims from similar kinds of sources. I scroll, then stop. What is missing? I cannot see why one story comes before another. I worry the order may serve clicks and ad money, not just my understanding. I want different views, even when they challenge me. I can put a number to that fear: 60% of people in a U.S. survey worried that personalization might make them miss important information. My clicks may narrow what returns, but I cannot see or change the basic rules.

tension_reflection.text: Both readers start with the same hope: what appears in a feed should help them understand the world. Then the stakes split. One is protecting a manageable morning and a sense of control over a personal news route. The other is protecting contact with views outside that route. Their power is not equal. One can follow, hide, or ask for more or less. The other cannot see or change the rules behind the ranking, even though those rules may shape what stays outside view.

in_one_line.text: This is not simply a fight over whether personalized news is good or bad. It is a question about the borders of a daily picture of the world: who can adjust them, and who can even see where they are. Convenience and concern are 2 experiences of the same hidden route through public news.
